title: Heidelberg Catechism
description: The Heidelberg Catechism (1563) — a confession of faith in 52 Lord's Days

questions.question_text: What is your only comfort in life and death?
questions.answer_text: That I am not my own, but belong — body and soul, in life and in death — to my faithful Savior, Jesus Christ. He has fully paid for all my sins with his precious blood, and has set me free from the tyranny of the devil. He also watches over me in such a way that not a hair can fall from my head without the will of my Father in heaven; in fact, all things must work together for my salvation. Because I belong to him, Christ, by his Holy Spirit, assures me of eternal life and makes me wholeheartedly willing and ready from now on to live for him.

prompts.prompt_text: What word in that answer surprised you the first time you read it?
Some people hold this comfort differently in hard seasons — has anyone experienced that gap between knowing it and feeling it?
That's worth a whole conversation on its own — for now, what does 'not my own' feel like on an ordinary Tuesday?

questions.question_text: How many things must you know that you may live and die happily?
questions.answer_text: Three things: first, the greatness of my sin and wretchedness; second, how I am freed from all my sins and their wretched consequences; third, what gratitude I owe to God for such redemption.

prompts.prompt_text: Which of the three — sin, redemption, gratitude — do you find it easiest to skip past?
Good thought — what do others think? Does the order of those three things matter, or could they come in any sequence?
Let's hold that and come back — if gratitude is the third thing, what does it actually look like in a regular week?

questions.question_text: Where do you know your sin and misery from?
questions.answer_text: From the law of God.

prompts.prompt_text: The answer is just four words. What's striking about how short it is?
Has anyone had a moment where the law showed them something about themselves they hadn't seen before?
Let's bring it back — if the law is a mirror, what does it reflect that we'd rather not see?

questions.question_text: What does God's law require of us?
questions.answer_text: Christ teaches us this in a summary in Matthew 22:37–40: Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind. This is the first and greatest commandment. And the second is like it: Love your neighbor as yourself. All the Law and the Prophets hang on these two commandments.

prompts.prompt_text: Jesus says 'all your heart, soul, and mind.' Which of those three do you find hardest to bring to God?
That's a strong point — let's see if anyone else wants to add to it. Does 'love your neighbor as yourself' assume you already love yourself?
Good — let's mark that and keep going. If this is what God requires, what does question 5 have to say next?

questions.question_text: Can you keep all this perfectly?
questions.answer_text: No. I have a natural tendency to hate God and my neighbor.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism doesn't say 'I try but fall short' — it says 'I hate.' What's the difference?
This is a hard one to sit with. Has anyone wrestled with what it means that this tendency is called 'natural'?
Let's stay close to the text — if the answer is simply 'no,' how does that change what we're hoping for from ourselves?

questions.question_text: Did God create man evil and perverse?
questions.answer_text: No. God created man good and in his image, that is, in true righteousness and holiness, so that he might rightly know God his creator, love him with all his heart, and live with him in eternal blessedness to praise and glorify him.

prompts.prompt_text: If God made man good, where does that leave us when we say 'that's just human nature'?
The answer says man was made 'to live with God in eternal blessedness' — does anyone have a sense of what that might have looked like before the fall?
Interesting angle — let's bring it back. If this is who we were made to be, how does it change how we think about who we are now?

questions.question_text: Then where does man's corrupt nature come from?
questions.answer_text: From the fall and disobedience of our first parents, Adam and Eve, in Paradise, whereby our human nature became so corrupt that we are all conceived and born in sin.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism says 'conceived and born in sin' — not just that we sin, but that we start broken. How does that land with you?
Good — let's hear from someone else. Does it feel fair that Adam's choice affects all of us?
Let's hold that and look at question 8 — what does it say follows from this?

questions.question_text: Are we so corrupt that we are totally unable to do any good and inclined toward all evil?
questions.answer_text: Yes, unless we are regenerated by the Spirit of God.

prompts.prompt_text: The answer is 'yes — unless.' What is the weight of that 'unless'?
Total inability is a strong claim. Has anyone wrestled with how to hold it while still feeling responsible for their choices?
Worth coming back to — for now, what does regeneration by the Spirit actually change, according to this answer?

questions.question_text: Does God not do man an injustice by requiring of him in his law what he cannot do?
questions.answer_text: No, for God created man able to do it; but man, at the instigation of the devil, in deliberate disobedience robbed himself and all his descendants of these gifts.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism says man robbed himself — does it feel different to hear it framed that way rather than as something that just happened to us?
Has anyone ever felt like God's standards were unfair before reading this answer?
Let's stay with the catechism's logic — if we were made able, what does that say about our responsibility now?

questions.question_text: Will God allow such disobedience and apostasy to go unpunished?
questions.answer_text: Certainly not. He is terribly displeased with our inborn as well as actual sins and will punish them by a just judgment in time and eternity, as He has declared: Cursed is everyone who does not observe and obey all the things written in the book of the law.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism uses the word 'terribly' — what does it do to you to hear that God is terribly displeased?
This is a hard truth — why does the catechism think it matters that we hear this before hearing about salvation?
That's worth exploring later — for now, how does knowing God is just change how we hear his mercy?

questions.question_text: But is God not also merciful?
questions.answer_text: God is indeed merciful, but he is also just. His justice requires that sin committed against the most high majesty of God be punished with the most severe — that is, with everlasting punishment of body and soul.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism doesn't let mercy cancel justice — why does it insist both must be satisfied?
Some people grew up hearing only mercy or only judgment — which side did you hear more of, and how does this answer sit with you?
Good — that tension is exactly where Lord's Day 5 picks up, so let's keep it with us as we move forward.

questions.question_text: Since, then, by the righteous judgment of God we deserve temporal and eternal punishment, is there any way by which we can escape this punishment and be again received into favor?
questions.answer_text: God wills that his justice be satisfied; therefore payment in full must be made to his justice, either by ourselves or by another.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism frames salvation as a payment problem — how does that legal framing help or complicate your understanding of the gospel?
Notice the catechism says 'either by ourselves or by another' — what does it feel like to sit with that either/or before the answer comes?
Let's stay on the catechism's logic — if God wills justice be satisfied, what does that rule out?

questions.question_text: Can we ourselves make this payment?
questions.answer_text: Certainly not. On the contrary, we increase our debt every day.

prompts.prompt_text: The answer says we make it worse every day — does that feel honest to you, or does it feel too harsh?
This is a short answer with a long shadow — what emotion does it surface for you?
Helpful — let's hear from someone else. Does the debt image resonate with you or does a different picture help more?

questions.question_text: Can any mere creature make the payment for us?
questions.answer_text: No. First, God will not punish any other creature for the sin which man has committed. Besides, no mere creature can bear the burden of God's eternal wrath against sin and deliver others from it.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism rules out all creatures — including angels. Why does infinite wrath require more than the best creature can give?
Has anyone ever hoped that a good life, a good person, or a good religion could be enough — and what does this answer say to that hope?
Good question — let's stay with it. If no creature can do it, who can, and where does that leave us?

questions.question_text: Then what kind of mediator and deliverer must we seek?
questions.answer_text: One who is a true and righteous man and yet more powerful than all creatures — that is, one who is also true God.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism says the mediator must be both truly human and truly God — why does each nature matter for what he has to do?
We haven't named Jesus yet — the catechism is building to him. How does the slow build affect how you hear the answer when it comes?
Let's hold that and see how Lord's Day 6 fills in the portrait of this mediator.

questions.question_text: Why must the mediator be a true and righteous man?
questions.answer_text: Because the justice of God requires that the same human nature which has sinned should pay for sin; but no one who is himself a sinner can pay for others.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism says human nature must pay because human nature sinned — how does that logic shape what you think the incarnation accomplished?
What does it mean to you that the one who paid was also 'righteous' — not just human, but truly righteous?
Good — let's keep the two requirements together. He had to be human and righteous — why does both matter?

questions.question_text: Why must he at the same time be true God?
questions.answer_text: So that by the power of his divine nature he might bear in his humanity the burden of God's wrath, and might obtain for us and restore to us righteousness and life.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism says divine power was needed to bear what no creature could — what does that say about the cross?
In your own words, what would have been missing if Jesus had been only a perfect human?
Let's get a second voice here — does anyone feel this in a different way than what was just shared?

questions.question_text: But who is that Mediator who is at the same time true God and a true and righteous man?
questions.answer_text: Our Lord Jesus Christ, who has been given to us for complete redemption and righteousness.

prompts.prompt_text: After five Lord's Days building the case, the catechism finally names him — what does it feel like to arrive at 'Jesus Christ' after all that setup?
The answer says he was 'given to us' — not earned, not achieved. What does gift language do to how you receive him?
Let's stay on 'complete redemption' — what would incomplete redemption look like, and why does it matter that it is complete?

questions.question_text: From where do you know this?
questions.answer_text: From the Holy Gospel, which God himself first revealed in Paradise; afterwards he had it proclaimed by the patriarchs and prophets, and foreshadowed by the sacrifices and other ceremonies of the law; and finally he fulfilled it through his only Son.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism traces the gospel all the way back to Eden — how does it change your reading of the Old Testament to see it as gospel-announcement?
God first revealed the gospel 'in Paradise' — right at the moment of the fall. What does the timing of that announcement tell you about God?
Worth pursuing — for now, what is the one thread the catechism says runs from Genesis to Christ?

questions.question_text: Are all men then restored by Christ just as they fell through Adam?
questions.answer_text: No. Only those are restored who by true faith are grafted into Christ and accept all his benefits.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism says 'only those who are grafted in' — how do you hold that alongside the breadth of God's love for the world?
The word 'grafted' is organic and permanent — what does that image say about how faith connects us to Christ?
That's a real tension — let's pin it and look at what the catechism means by 'true faith' in the next question.

questions.question_text: What is true faith?
questions.answer_text: True faith is not only a certain knowledge by which I accept as true all that God has revealed in his Word, but also a firm confidence that not only to others, but to me also, forgiveness of sins, everlasting righteousness, and salvation are freely given by God, out of mere grace, only for the sake of Christ's merits.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism insists faith is personal — not just 'to others, but to me also.' Where does that personal confidence feel easy or hard for you?
Knowledge plus confidence — why does the catechism insist both are needed? What happens to faith if you only have one?
Helpful — let's hear from someone who finds the confidence part harder than the knowledge part.

questions.question_text: What, then, must a Christian believe?
questions.answer_text: All that is promised us in the Gospel, which the articles of our catholic and undoubted Christian faith teach us in summary.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism calls the Creed a summary of the gospel — does that change how you feel when you recite it in worship?
What word or phrase in the Apostles' Creed is most alive for you right now, and which feels most distant?
Good — let's stay with 'all that is promised.' What does it mean that we believe promises, not just propositions?

questions.question_text: What are these articles?
questions.answer_text: I believe in God the Father Almighty, Maker of heaven and earth. And in Jesus Christ, his only begotten Son, our Lord; who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the virgin Mary; suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, dead, and buried; he descended into hell; the third day he rose from the dead; he ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of God the Father Almighty; from there he shall come to judge the living and the dead. I believe in the Holy Spirit; the holy catholic Church; the communion of saints; the forgiveness of sins; the resurrection of the body; and the life everlasting. Amen.

prompts.prompt_text: Read the Creed aloud together, then ask: which article did you most need to hear today?
Is there any line in the Creed you find yourself saying without quite believing it yet — and what would it take to own it?
Let's keep those questions with us — the next several Lord's Days walk through the Creed article by article.

questions.question_text: How are these articles divided?
questions.answer_text: Into three parts: the first is about God the Father and our creation; the second about God the Son and our redemption; the third about God the Holy Spirit and our sanctification.

prompts.prompt_text: Creation, redemption, sanctification — three works, one God. Which of the three do you tend to think about most, and which do you neglect?
Is there a person of the Trinity you feel closest to, and one who feels more distant or abstract to you?
Let's bring it back — the catechism ties each person to a specific work in our lives. How does that structure help you pray?

questions.question_text: Since there is but one God, why do you speak of three: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit?
questions.answer_text: Because God has so revealed himself in his Word that these three distinct persons are the one, true, eternal God.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism grounds the Trinity in revelation, not philosophy — does that feel like solid footing to you, or do you want more explanation?
The Trinity is mysterious — what is one thing about it that actually comforts you rather than confuses you?
Good — now let's hear from someone who finds the Trinity harder to explain than to believe.

questions.question_text: What do you believe when you say: I believe in God the Father Almighty, Maker of heaven and earth?
questions.answer_text: That the eternal Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who out of nothing created heaven and earth with all that is in them, who also upholds and governs them by his eternal counsel and providence, is for the sake of Christ his Son my God and my Father. I trust in him so completely that I have no doubt that he will provide me with all things necessary for body and soul. Moreover, whatever evil he sends upon me in this valley of sorrow I will turn to my good, for he is able to do it, being Almighty God, and willing also, being a faithful Father.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism says 'I have no doubt' — is that a description of your experience, an aspiration, or something else?
The phrase 'this valley of sorrow' is honest about life — how does it feel to have that realism inside a statement of faith?
Let's stay with the catechism's claim that we know God as Father only through Christ — how does that shape what we can expect from him?

questions.question_text: What do you understand by the providence of God?
questions.answer_text: The almighty and ever-present power of God by which he still upholds, as it were by his own hand, heaven and earth together with all creatures, and rules in such a way that leaves and grass, rain and drought, fruitful and unfruitful years, food and drink, health and sickness, riches and poverty, and everything else come to us not by chance but by his fatherly hand.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism lists sickness and poverty alongside food and health as coming from God's hand — how does that sit with you?
What event in your life would be most changed if you truly believed it came through God's fatherly hand rather than by chance?
The problem of evil is real — for now, let's see what the catechism says this belief is supposed to produce in us in the next question.

questions.question_text: How does the knowledge of God's creation and providence benefit us?
questions.answer_text: We learn that we are to be patient in adversity, thankful in prosperity, and with a view to the future we are to have good confidence in our faithful God and Father that no creature shall separate us from his love, since all creatures are so completely in his hand that without his will they cannot so much as move.

prompts.prompt_text: Patient in adversity, thankful in prosperity — which of the two do you find harder, and why?
The catechism says 'no creature shall separate us from his love' — what creature or circumstance most threatens that confidence for you right now?
Let's land there — if nothing can move without God's will, what does that do to your anxiety about the future?

questions.question_text: Why is the Son of God called Jesus, that is, Savior?
questions.answer_text: Because he saves us from all our sins, and because salvation is not to be sought or found in any other.

prompts.prompt_text: His name means Savior — how often does that meaning shape how you actually address him when you pray?
The catechism says 'all our sins' — not some, not the manageable ones. What does 'all' do for you?
Good — let's hear what 'no other' means to someone else in the group.

questions.question_text: Do those who seek their salvation and well-being from saints, themselves, or anywhere else really believe in the only Savior Jesus?
questions.answer_text: No. Although they boast of him in words, they in fact deny the only Savior Jesus; for one of two things must be true: either Jesus is not a complete Savior, or those who by true faith accept this Savior must find in him all that is necessary for their salvation.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism says adding anything to Jesus is functionally denying him — where do you see that temptation, in yourself or around you?
Either Jesus is complete or he is not — why does the catechism say there is no middle ground here?
Let's stay with the practical question — what does it look like in daily life to find everything necessary in him?

questions.question_text: Why is he called Christ, that is, Anointed?
questions.answer_text: Because he is ordained of God the Father and anointed with the Holy Spirit to be our chief Prophet and Teacher, who has fully revealed to us the secret counsel and will of God concerning our redemption; to be our only High Priest, who by the one sacrifice of his body has redeemed us, and who continually intercedes for us with the Father; and to be our eternal King, who governs us by his Word and Spirit, and who defends and preserves us in the redemption obtained for us.

prompts.prompt_text: Prophet, priest, and king — which of those three roles of Christ is most alive for you right now, and which do you draw on least?
The catechism says he 'continually intercedes' — what does it mean to you that Jesus is praying for you right now?
Let's come back — how does each role address a specific kind of need we have?

questions.question_text: But why are you called a Christian?
questions.answer_text: Because I am a member of Christ by faith, and thus am partaker of his anointing, so that I may confess his name, may present myself a living sacrifice of thankfulness to him, and may fight with a free and good conscience against sin and the devil in this life, and hereafter in eternity reign with him over all creatures.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism says Christians share in Christ's anointing — prophet, priest, and king applies to us too. How does that change how you think about your ordinary week?
Fighting 'with a free and good conscience' — does your conscience feel free right now, or is something weighing it down?
Good — let's land there. If Christians share Christ's anointing, what is one concrete thing that implies for how you live this week?

questions.question_text: Why is Christ called God's only begotten Son, since we also are children of God?
questions.answer_text: Because Christ alone is the eternal, natural Son of God; we, however, are adopted children of God by grace through Christ.

prompts.prompt_text: Adopted by grace versus eternally begotten — how does understanding the difference change how you think about your relationship to God?
For some people adoption feels like second-best. What does the New Testament say about the full status of adopted children in God's family?
Let's stay with the catechism's logic — our sonship depends entirely on his. What does that dependency feel like to you?

questions.question_text: Why do you call him our Lord?
questions.answer_text: Because he has redeemed us, body and soul, from all our sins, not with silver or gold but with his precious blood, and has delivered us from all the power of the devil, and has made us his own possession.

prompts.prompt_text: Lordship here is grounded in redemption — he is Lord because he bought us. How does that change what it means to submit to his authority?
The catechism says 'body and soul' — both are redeemed. What does it mean to you that your body is not left out?
Good — let's hear how someone else responds to being called his 'possession.'

questions.question_text: What do you understand by: conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the virgin Mary?
questions.answer_text: That the eternal Son of God, who is and remains true and eternal God, took upon himself true human nature from the flesh and blood of the virgin Mary by the work of the Holy Spirit, so that he might also be the true seed of David, like his brothers in every respect, yet without sin.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism says he is 'like his brothers in every respect, yet without sin' — what does it mean to you that Jesus understands human experience from the inside?
Which part of the incarnation is hardest for you to believe — that he is fully God, that he is fully human, or that he is both at once?
Good question — let's stay with what the catechism emphasizes: what did he take on, and what does that cost him?

questions.question_text: What benefit do you receive from the holy conception and birth of Christ?
questions.answer_text: That he is our Mediator, and that he covers, in the sight of God, the sin in which I was conceived and born.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism says his birth covers our birth-in-sin — his beginning undoes the curse on ours. How does that land?
What does it mean practically that Jesus covers the sin we were born into — not just the sins we commit?
Let's hold that. How does the answer connect to what we said about original sin back in Lord's Day 3?

questions.question_text: What do you understand by the word suffered?
questions.answer_text: That throughout his life on earth, but especially at the end of it, he bore in body and soul the wrath of God against the sin of the whole human race, so that by his suffering, as the only atoning sacrifice, he might redeem our body and soul from everlasting damnation, and obtain for us God's grace, righteousness, and eternal life.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism says his suffering was not just at the cross but throughout his life — how does that expand your understanding of what he endured for us?
He bore the wrath against 'the whole human race' — including yours. What happens in you when you make that personal?
Let's stay with the catechism's claim — it says both body and soul were involved. Why does that matter?

questions.question_text: Why did he suffer under Pontius Pilate as judge?
questions.answer_text: So that he, being innocent, might be condemned by the temporal judge, and thereby free us from the severe judgment of God that was to fall on us.

prompts.prompt_text: An innocent man condemned so the guilty go free — how does the injustice of that moment serve God's justice?
Why does the catechism make a point of the human judge? What does it matter that this happened in history under a named official?
Good — let's hear another voice. What strikes you most about the fact that he was 'condemned' specifically?

questions.question_text: Does it have a special meaning that he was crucified and did not die in a different way?
questions.answer_text: Yes, for thereby I am assured that he took upon himself the curse which lay upon me, since death on the cross was cursed by God.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism says the method of death matters — he had to be cursed so the curse on us could be removed. How does knowing that change how you see the cross?
Is there something in your life that has felt cursed or unredeemable? How does this answer speak to that?
Let's hold that and move into Lord's Day 16, where the catechism goes to his death and burial.

questions.question_text: Why was it necessary for Christ to humble himself even to death?
questions.answer_text: Because the justice and truth of God required that satisfaction for our sins could be made in no other way than by the death of the Son of God.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism says there was no other way — what does it do to you to hear that God saw no path around the death of his Son?
The word 'humble' is used of death — the highest humbling himself to the lowest point. Where does that move you?
Good — let's stay with necessity. Why could God not simply forgive without satisfaction?

questions.question_text: Why was he buried?
questions.answer_text: His burial testified that he had really died.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism treats the burial as proof — why does it matter that the death was real and not symbolic?
The Creed mentions the burial — we often rush past it. What does sitting with the fact of his burial do for you?
Good — let's get a shorter answer from someone else. One word: what does the burial of Jesus mean to you?

questions.question_text: Since Christ has died for us, why must we also die?
questions.answer_text: Our death is not a payment for our sins, but only a dying to sins and an entering into eternal life.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism reframes death as a door, not a penalty — how does that change your relationship to your own mortality?
Paul says to live is Christ and to die is gain — do you believe the second half as much as the first?
Worth exploring — for now, the catechism says our death is not payment. Who already paid, and what does that change?

questions.question_text: What further benefit do we receive from the sacrifice and death of Christ on the cross?
questions.answer_text: That by his power our old man is crucified, put to death, and buried with him, so that the evil lusts of the flesh may no longer reign in us, but that we may offer ourselves to him as a sacrifice of thankfulness.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism says the old man is crucified — not just forgiven, but killed. Where do you most need to believe that is true of you?
Why does the catechism connect his death to our daily battle with sin? What is the link?
Let's land there — how do you offer yourself as a sacrifice of thankfulness in a way that does not feel like performance?

questions.question_text: Why is there added: he descended into hell?
questions.answer_text: That in my greatest temptations I may be assured that Christ my Lord, by his inexpressible anguish, pain, terror, and agony which he endured throughout all his sufferings but especially on the cross, has delivered me from the anguish and torment of hell.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism interprets 'descended into hell' as the depth of his inner anguish — how does that affect your understanding of what Jesus experienced at Golgotha?
The catechism says this article is for your 'greatest temptations' — what does it mean to reach for this truth when you are at your lowest?
Let's stay with the comfort the catechism intends here — how does Christ's descent into anguish give you confidence when you face your darkest moments?

questions.question_text: What benefit do we receive from the resurrection of Christ?
questions.answer_text: First, by his resurrection he has overcome death, that he might make us partakers of that righteousness which he has obtained for us by his death. Second, by his power we are already raised to a new life. Third, the resurrection of Christ is to us a sure pledge of our blessed resurrection.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism gives three resurrection benefits — righteousness, new life now, and future resurrection. Which one is most real to you today?
The catechism says we are 'already raised' — not just waiting to be. What would change in your daily life if you lived from that reality?
Good — let's stay with what the catechism calls a 'sure pledge.' How does his resurrection become grounds for our confidence?

questions.question_text: How do you understand the words: he ascended into heaven?
questions.answer_text: That Christ, in the sight of his disciples, was taken up from the earth into heaven, and continues there on our behalf until he shall come again to judge the living and the dead.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism says he is there 'on our behalf' right now — how often does the present intercession of the ascended Christ shape how you pray?
The disciples watched him go and were told he would return — how do you hold the 'now' and 'not yet' of the ascension in your own faith?
Let's stay with what the catechism says he is doing there — why does it matter that he 'continues on our behalf'?

questions.question_text: Then is Christ not with us until the end of the world, as he has promised?
questions.answer_text: Christ is true man and true God. With respect to his human nature he is no more on earth, but with respect to his divinity, majesty, grace, and Spirit he is never absent from us.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism distinguishes his human nature from his divine presence — how do you experience Christ's presence if his body is in heaven?
Why does it matter to hold both: that he is bodily in heaven and that he is never absent from us?
In a moment when God feels distant, which of these two truths is harder to hold — his heavenly location or his promised presence?

questions.question_text: But are not the two natures in Christ separated from each other in this way, if the humanity is not wherever the divinity is?
questions.answer_text: Not at all, for since divinity is incomprehensible and everywhere present, it must follow that divinity is indeed beyond the bounds of the humanity which it has assumed, and yet is nonetheless within this humanity as well, and remains personally united to it.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism says divinity is both beyond and within the humanity — not separated from it. Why does the unity of Christ's two natures matter for what he can do for us?
Let's hear from someone for whom this question is genuinely puzzling — what do you find hardest to hold here?
Good — the catechism's point is that the natures are not separated. Why would it matter if they were?

questions.question_text: What benefit do we receive from Christ's ascension into heaven?
questions.answer_text: First, that he is our advocate in the presence of his Father in heaven. Second, that we have our flesh in heaven as a sure pledge that he, as the Head, will also take us, his members, up to himself. Third, that he sends us his Spirit as a counterpart pledge, by whose power we seek what is above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God, and not the things that are on earth.

prompts.prompt_text: Three benefits: advocate, pledge of our resurrection, Spirit as gift — which of these three most changes how you think about Jesus being gone from earth?
Human flesh is now in heaven — permanently. What does it mean that our nature is already where we are headed?
Let's land on the Spirit — the catechism says he is a 'counterpart pledge.' What is the Spirit pledging to us?

sessions.title: Lord's Day 19
sessions.theme: At the Right Hand of God

questions.question_text: Why is it added: and sits at the right hand of God?
questions.answer_text: Because Christ ascended into heaven for this reason: that he might there appear as the Head of his Church, through whom the Father governs all things.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism says Christ governs all things from the right hand of the Father — how does that affect how you think about politics, suffering, and the news?
He is Head of the Church — your church is under his governance. What would it look like to lead or participate from that reality?
Let's stay with the catechism's scope — it says 'all things,' not just church things. What does universal governance mean for your daily life?

questions.question_text: What benefit does this glory of Christ our Head give to us?
questions.answer_text: First, that through his Holy Spirit he pours out heavenly gifts upon us his members. Second, that by his power he defends us and keeps us safe from all enemies.

prompts.prompt_text: Gifts and defense — the catechism says his enthronement benefits you right now. Which of those two do you most need to believe today?
The catechism says he 'keeps us safe from all enemies' — what enemy most threatens you right now, and what does it mean to trust his protection?
Good — let's hear from someone else. What heavenly gift feels most alive in your life right now?

questions.question_text: What comfort is it to you that Christ shall come to judge the living and the dead?
questions.answer_text: That in all affliction and persecution I may await with head held high the very Judge from heaven who has already submitted himself to the judgment of God for me and has removed all the curse from me; who shall cast all his enemies and mine into everlasting condemnation, but shall take me with all his chosen ones to himself into heavenly joy and glory.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism calls the last judgment a comfort, not a threat — does it feel that way to you, and what would need to be true for it to?
The Judge is the one who was already judged in your place — how does that identity change the verdict you expect?
Let's stay with the catechism's surprising move — it turns judgment into hope. What makes that possible, according to the answer?

sessions.title: Lord's Day 21
sessions.theme: The Holy Spirit and the Church

questions.question_text: What do you believe about the Holy Spirit?
questions.answer_text: First, he is, together with the Father and the Son, true and eternal God. Second, he is also given to me personally; by true faith he makes me a partaker of Christ and all his benefits, comforts me, and shall abide with me forever.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism says the Spirit is given 'to me personally' — how personal does your experience of the Holy Spirit actually feel?
The Spirit's job here is to make Christ's benefits yours — which benefit most needs to feel more real to you right now?
Let's come back — the catechism says he shall abide with you forever. What does permanence mean for how you relate to him?

questions.question_text: What do you believe about the holy catholic Christian Church?
questions.answer_text: That out of the whole human race, from the beginning to the end of the world, the Son of God, by his Spirit and Word, gathers, defends, and preserves for himself a community chosen for eternal life and united in true faith. And I am and forever shall remain a living member of this community.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism says the Church spans all of history — how does knowing you belong to something that stretches from Abel to the last believer change how you think about your local congregation?
'I am and forever shall remain a living member' — does that feel like a promise or a challenge to you right now?
Good — let's hear how someone else thinks about what it means to be 'gathered' rather than just showing up.

questions.question_text: What do you understand by the communion of saints?
questions.answer_text: First, that believers, all and everyone, as members of Christ have communion with him and share in all his treasures and gifts. Second, that everyone is obliged to use these gifts willingly and joyfully for the benefit and well-being of the other members.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism says communion with saints flows from communion with Christ — you cannot have one without the other. How does that challenge any private Christianity?
The catechism uses the word 'obliged' — we are not just invited but required to use our gifts for others. How does obligation sit alongside joy in this answer?
What gift do you have right now that someone else in this group most needs — and what makes it hard to offer it?

questions.question_text: What do you believe about the forgiveness of sins?
questions.answer_text: That for the sake of Christ's satisfaction, God will no longer remember my sins or the sinfulness with which I have to struggle all my life long, but graciously grants me the righteousness of Christ, so that I shall never come into condemnation.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism says God will 'no longer remember' your sins — not just forgive, but forget. Does that feel too good to be true?
It also says God forgives the sinfulness you 'have to struggle with all your life long' — not just past sins but ongoing patterns. What does that do for you?
Let's land on 'never come into condemnation' — what would change in your daily life if you believed that without qualification?

questions.question_text: What comfort does the resurrection of the body offer you?
questions.answer_text: That not only shall my soul after this life be immediately taken up to Christ my Head, but also my very flesh, raised by the power of Christ, shall be reunited with my soul and made conformable to the glorious body of Christ.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism says your body — this body — will be raised and made like Christ's glorious body. How does that change how you treat and think about your physical self?
Job said 'in my flesh I shall see God' — for someone who has suffered in their body, what does the resurrection of the body mean?
Good question — let's stay with the catechism's emphasis on the body specifically. Why does Christianity insist on bodily resurrection, not just spiritual survival?

questions.question_text: What comfort do you receive from the article about life everlasting?
questions.answer_text: That since I now feel in my heart the beginning of eternal joy, after this life I shall possess perfect blessedness, such as eye has not seen nor ear heard, nor the heart of man conceived — and this in order to praise God forever.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism says you already feel 'the beginning of eternal joy' now — do you? Where do you notice it?
Eye has not seen, ear has not heard — what does it do for your daily endurance to know the destination is beyond anything you can currently imagine?
Let's hear from someone who finds it hard to feel that beginning of joy right now — what gets in the way?

questions.question_text: But what does it help you now to believe all this?
questions.answer_text: In Christ I am righteous before God and an heir of eternal life.

prompts.prompt_text: After twenty-two Lord's Days of doctrine, the catechism asks 'what does it help you?' — how well does your belief connect to your daily life?
'Righteous before God' — not working toward it, but already there in Christ. What is your gut response to that claim?
Good — let's stay with 'heir of eternal life.' What do heirs do before they receive the inheritance?

questions.question_text: How are you righteous before God?
questions.answer_text: Only by true faith in Jesus Christ. Even though my conscience accuses me that I have grievously sinned against all God's commandments and have not kept any of them, and even though I am still inclined toward all evil, nevertheless, without any merit of my own, out of mere grace, God grants and credits to me the perfect satisfaction, righteousness, and holiness of Christ, as if I had never sinned nor been a sinner, as if I had been as perfectly obedient as Christ was obedient for me — if only I accept this gift with a believing heart.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism holds two things in one answer: your conscience accuses you, and yet God credits you with Christ's righteousness. How do you live in that tension?
The catechism says God treats you 'as if you had never sinned' — is that a legal fiction, or is it a deeper reality? What makes it true?
Let's stay with the catechism's phrase 'mere grace' — what does 'mere' mean there, and why is it important?

questions.question_text: Why do you say that you are righteous by faith alone?
questions.answer_text: Not that I am acceptable to God on account of the worthiness of my faith, for only the satisfaction, righteousness, and holiness of Christ is my righteousness before God; I can receive this righteousness and make it my own by faith only.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism clarifies that faith itself is not the merit — Christ is. How does that prevent faith from becoming another work?
Has your faith ever felt too weak to save you? What does this answer say to that fear?
Let's hear from someone who grew up thinking strong faith was the point — how does this answer reframe that?

questions.question_text: But why cannot our good works be our righteousness before God, or at least a part of it?
questions.answer_text: Because the righteousness which can stand before the judgment of God must be absolutely perfect and in complete agreement with the law of God, whereas even our best works in this life are all imperfect and defiled with sin.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism says even our best works are defiled — how does that land with you, and what keeps us from despair?
When you imagine standing before God, do you still feel the pull to point to something you have done? What does the catechism say about that?
Good — let's stay with the standard. What is 'absolutely perfect' and who meets it?

questions.question_text: But do our good works earn nothing, even though God promises to reward them in this life and the life to come?
questions.answer_text: This reward is not given because of merit, but out of grace.

prompts.prompt_text: God rewards good works but not as merit — how is a gracious reward different from an earned wage, and does the distinction matter to you?
If your good works are rewarded out of grace, not merit, does that make doing them feel more or less meaningful to you?
Let's keep that question with us and look at why this doctrine does not produce laziness — question 64 addresses it directly.

questions.question_text: But does this doctrine not make men careless and profane?
questions.answer_text: No, for it is impossible that those who are grafted into Christ by true faith should not bring forth fruits of thankfulness.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism says fruit is inevitable for those in Christ — not optional or occasional but impossible to be absent. Does that match your experience?
Why does the catechism use 'impossible' — is that too strong, or is it the right word?
Let's stay with the image — a branch grafted into a vine produces fruit because of the vine, not because of its own effort. What does that say about where our good works come from?

questions.question_text: Since then only faith makes us share in Christ and all his benefits, where does this faith come from?
questions.answer_text: From the Holy Spirit, who kindles true faith in our hearts by the preaching of the Holy Gospel, and strengthens it by the use of the Holy Sacraments.

prompts.prompt_text: Faith comes from preaching and sacraments — the Spirit works through means. How seriously do you take those means in your own life?
Can you trace the Spirit's kindling of faith in your life to a specific sermon, conversation, or moment at the table?
Let's stay with the catechism's point — God is not random about how he gives faith. Why does it matter that he uses Word and sacrament?

questions.question_text: What are the Sacraments?
questions.answer_text: The Sacraments are visible, holy signs and seals instituted by God in order that by their use he might the more fully declare and seal to us the promise of the Gospel — namely, that out of free grace he grants us forgiveness of sins and everlasting life for the sake of the one sacrifice of Christ accomplished on the cross.

prompts.prompt_text: Signs and seals — a sign points, a seal confirms. How does the sacrament do both of those things at once?
The catechism says the sacraments add to what the Word does — they declare 'more fully.' What do they do that preaching alone cannot?
When did a sacrament last feel like a seal to you rather than a routine?

questions.question_text: Are both the Word and the Sacraments then intended to direct our faith to the sacrifice of Jesus Christ on the cross as the only ground of our salvation?
questions.answer_text: Yes indeed, for the Holy Spirit teaches in the Gospel and assures us by the holy Sacraments that our whole salvation rests in the one sacrifice of Christ made for us on the cross.

prompts.prompt_text: Both Word and sacrament point to the cross — nothing else. How does that singular focus shape what you expect from a sermon or the Lord's Supper?
Let's hear from someone who finds the cross-focus more challenging than comforting — why?
Let's land there. If the whole point of means of grace is to press Christ's sacrifice into us, what should we leave with every Sunday?

questions.question_text: How many Sacraments has Christ instituted in the New Testament?
questions.answer_text: Two: Holy Baptism and the Holy Supper.

prompts.prompt_text: Two sacraments, not seven — one at the beginning of the Christian life and one that sustains it throughout. How do those two bookmarks shape a life of faith?
Which sacrament has been more meaningful to you personally, and which have you taken for granted?
Good — let's stay with the catechism's point. Christ instituted exactly these two. What does his specific intention tell us about what God wants us to have?

questions.question_text: How does Holy Baptism signify and seal to you that the one sacrifice of Christ on the cross benefits you?
questions.answer_text: In this way: Christ has instituted this external washing with water and by it has promised that I am as certainly washed from the impurity of my soul — that is, from all my sins — by his blood and Spirit as I am washed externally with water, which is ordinarily used to remove bodily impurity.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism says your baptism is a promise God made to you — as certain as the water that touched you. How often do you return to that certainty?
Have you ever drawn comfort from your baptism in a dark moment, or does it mostly feel like something in the past?
Let's stay with the ordinary — washing is something you do every day. Why does the catechism use that image for the most extraordinary thing God does?

questions.question_text: What does it mean to be washed with the blood and Spirit of Christ?
questions.answer_text: It means to have the forgiveness of sins from God through grace, for the sake of Christ's blood which he shed for us in his sacrifice on the cross; and also to be renewed by the Holy Spirit and sanctified as members of Christ, so that we may die more and more to sin and lead a holy and blameless life.

prompts.prompt_text: Blood and Spirit — forgiveness and renewal. The catechism holds both together. Which do you tend to emphasize more in your faith?
Why does renewal matter alongside forgiveness — what would be incomplete if God forgave us without also renewing us?
The catechism says we 'die more and more to sin' — ongoing, not completed. Where are you in that process right now?

questions.question_text: Where has Christ promised that he will wash us with his blood and Spirit as surely as we are washed with the water of baptism?
questions.answer_text: In the institution of baptism, where he says: Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. And: Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, but whoever does not believe will be condemned.

prompts.prompt_text: The promise is in Christ's own words at his institution of baptism — why does the catechism point you to the text rather than just to the feeling?
Good — let's hear from someone who finds it helpful to have a word from Christ himself behind the sacrament.
Let's keep that text with us. The promise is sure because it is his word — how does resting on a promise change your posture toward your baptism?

questions.question_text: Does this outward washing with water itself wash away sins?
questions.answer_text: No, only the blood of Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit cleanse us from all sins.

prompts.prompt_text: The water is a sign, not the thing itself — how do you hold the sign and the reality together without collapsing one into the other?
If the water does not wash sins, why does the catechism still insist we need it? What does the sign accomplish that the Spirit does not accomplish without it?
Good distinction — let's stay with the catechism's point. The water points to what? And who does the actual cleansing?

questions.question_text: Why then does the Holy Spirit call baptism the washing of regeneration and the washing away of sins?
questions.answer_text: God speaks in this way for a good reason: namely, not only to teach us that just as the filth of the body is taken away by water, so our sins are taken away by the blood and Spirit of Christ; but also, and above all, to assure us by this divine pledge and sign that we are as truly washed from our sins spiritually as our bodies are washed with water physically.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism says God calls baptism a washing 'for a good reason' — to teach and to assure. How are teaching and assurance different functions?
God uses physical, sensory language to communicate spiritual realities — what does it tell you that he meets us through our bodies?
The catechism says we are 'as truly' washed spiritually as we are physically. If you could feel that certainty right now, what would change?

questions.question_text: Should infants also be baptized?
questions.answer_text: Yes, because they, as well as adults, are included in the covenant and the church of God, and because both redemption from sin and the Holy Spirit, who produces faith, are promised to them no less than to adults. Baptism as the sign of the covenant should therefore be administered to them, as it was administered to the children of Israel through circumcision, which was the sign of the covenant in the old dispensation.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism grounds infant baptism in covenant inclusion — the same covenant, a new sign. How persuasive do you find that argument?
Whether you were baptized as an infant or as a believer, what does your baptism mean to you now?
This question divides Christians — let's stay with what the catechism claims about covenant promise. What is God saying to families who bring their children to baptism?

questions.question_text: How does the holy Supper signify and seal to you that you are a partaker of the one sacrifice of Christ on the cross and of all his benefits?
questions.answer_text: In this way: Christ has commanded me and all believers to eat this broken bread and drink this cup in remembrance of him, and has promised that his body was offered and broken on the cross for me and his blood was shed for me, as certainly as I see with my eyes the bread of the Lord broken for me and the cup given to me, and as certainly as I receive with my mouth the bread and the cup of the Lord as sure signs of the body and blood of Christ.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism says the bread is given 'for me' — as personally as you can see it and touch it. How personal does the Supper feel when you actually take it?
The Lord's Supper is supposed to be as certain as something you can see and taste — when did it last feel that certain to you?
Let's stay with the physicality — why does the catechism emphasize seeing and receiving with your mouth?

questions.question_text: What does it mean to eat the crucified body of Christ and to drink his shed blood?
questions.answer_text: First, to accept with a believing heart all the suffering and the death of Christ, and thereby to obtain forgiveness of sins and life eternal. Second, beyond that, to become more and more united to his sacred body by the Holy Spirit, who dwells both in Christ and in us; so that, even though Christ is in heaven and we are on earth, we are nevertheless flesh of his flesh and bone of his bone, and live and are governed eternally by one and the same Spirit.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism says eating is about accepting and becoming — faith and union. Which of those two do you experience more at the table?
The catechism says we are 'flesh of his flesh and bone of his bone' — borrowing marriage language. What does that kind of intimacy say about what the Supper is?
Christ is in heaven and you are on earth — and yet the catechism says you are governed by the same Spirit. What does that communion feel like in practice?

questions.question_text: Where has Christ promised that he will feed and nourish believers with his body and blood just as surely as they eat this broken bread and drink this cup?
questions.answer_text: In the institution of the Holy Supper: The Lord Jesus, on the night when he was betrayed, took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it, and said: This is my body, which is for you. Do this in remembrance of me. In the same way also the cup, after supper, saying: This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me.

prompts.prompt_text: He said these words on the night he was betrayed — what does the timing tell you about what kind of gift this is?
Let's hear from someone who thinks about 'remembrance' — what are we supposed to be remembering, and how does memory work here?
Let's hold those words. 'For you' — as simple as that. What do those two words do when you hear them at the table?

questions.question_text: Do the bread and wine become the very body and blood of Christ?
questions.answer_text: No. Just as the water of baptism is not changed into the blood of Christ nor becomes the washing away of sins itself, but is only a sign and seal of it, so too the bread of the Lord's Supper does not become the body of Christ itself, even though it is called the body of Christ in keeping with the nature and language of sacraments.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism is clear about what the bread is not — does that clarity help or diminish what the Supper means to you?
The catechism uses baptism as the parallel case. How does that comparison help explain what sacramental language is doing?
This is a real disagreement between Christians — let's stay with what the catechism affirms rather than what it denies. What does the bread truly give us?

questions.question_text: Why then does Christ call the bread his body and the cup his blood, or the new covenant in his blood, and why does Paul use the words a sharing in the body and blood of Christ?
questions.answer_text: Christ speaks in this way for good reason: not only to teach us that just as bread and wine sustain our temporal life, so his crucified body and shed blood are the true food and drink of our souls for eternal life; but also, and above all, to assure us by this visible sign and pledge that through the work of the Holy Spirit we really share in his true body and blood, just as truly as we receive with our mouths these holy signs in his remembrance, and that all his suffering and obedience are certainly our own, as if we ourselves had suffered and made satisfaction in our own person.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism says Christ's suffering and obedience are 'certainly our own, as if we ourselves had suffered' — how far does that identification go?
The Supper is described as food and drink for your soul — in what way do you feel spiritually nourished when you take it?
The catechism says the Spirit makes the sharing 'real' — not symbolic but actual. What would it mean to receive the Supper expecting that this week?

questions.question_text: What difference is there between the Lord's Supper and the papal Mass?
questions.answer_text: The Lord's Supper testifies to us that we have complete forgiveness of all our sins through the one sacrifice of Jesus Christ, which he himself accomplished on the cross once for all; and that we through the Holy Spirit are grafted into Christ, who with his true body is now in heaven at the right hand of the Father, and is there to be worshipped. But the Mass teaches that the living and the dead do not have forgiveness of sins through the suffering of Christ unless Christ is also daily offered for them by the priests; and that Christ is bodily present in the form of bread and wine and is therefore to be worshipped therein. And thus the Mass is fundamentally nothing other than a denial of the one sacrifice and suffering of Jesus Christ and an accursed idolatry.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism's strongest objection to the Mass is that it implies Christ's one sacrifice was incomplete — why does the finality of 'once for all' matter so much?
This question has a sharp polemical tone — let's focus on the positive. What does the Lord's Supper affirm that the catechism wants us to hold onto?
Good — let's hear from someone who has friends or family in a tradition that practices the Mass. How do you hold this catechism answer charitably?

questions.question_text: Who are to come to the table of the Lord?
questions.answer_text: Those who are displeased with themselves because of their sins, and yet trust that these sins have been forgiven them and that their remaining weakness is covered by the suffering and death of Christ; who also desire more and more to strengthen their faith and to lead a better life. Hypocrites and those who are not penitent, however, eat and drink judgment to themselves.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism says those who are 'displeased with themselves' belong at the table — it is not for those who have arrived. How does that change who you think the Supper is for?
Have you ever stayed away from the table because you felt too sinful to come? What does this answer say to that?

Let's hold both sides — those who trust despite weakness are invited; those who are impenitent should examine themselves. How do we hold that without making the table either too exclusive or too casual?

questions.question_text: Are those who show by their confession and life that they are unbelieving and ungodly also to be admitted to this Supper?
questions.answer_text: No, for thereby the covenant of God would be profaned and his wrath provoked against the whole congregation; therefore the Christian Church is obliged, according to the ordinance of Christ and his apostles, to exclude such persons by the use of the keys of the kingdom of heaven until they show amendment of life.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism says excluding unrepentant members protects the whole congregation — how do you think about discipline as an act of love rather than punishment?
Why does the catechism say fencing the table is an obligation, not just an option for the church?
Let's stay with the catechism's goal — the keys are for restoration, not permanent exclusion. What does 'amendment of life' as the condition tell us about the purpose of discipline?

questions.question_text: What are the keys of the kingdom of heaven?
questions.answer_text: The preaching of the Holy Gospel and Christian discipline or excommunication. By these two the kingdom of heaven is opened to believers and closed to unbelievers.

prompts.prompt_text: Two keys — preaching and discipline. How seriously does your church use both, and which tends to be neglected?
The catechism says the keys open and close — gospel preaching opens the kingdom to believers. Has a sermon ever felt like a door opening for you?
Let's stay with the catechism's structure — why does the kingdom need both opening and closing? What would be lost without either key?

questions.question_text: How is the kingdom of heaven opened and closed by the preaching of the Gospel?
questions.answer_text: According to the command of Christ, when it is proclaimed and openly testified to all and every believer that, as often and as long as they accept the Gospel promise with a true faith, all their sins are truly forgiven them by God for the sake of Christ's merits; and when it is testified to all unbelievers and hypocrites that the wrath of God and eternal condemnation rest upon them as long as they do not repent. According to this testimony of the Gospel, God will judge them, both in this and in the life to come.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism says preaching does something — it opens or closes the kingdom according to response. Does that give the sermon more weight than you usually assign it?
The preacher pronounces what God has already decided — how do we understand human proclamation having that kind of authority?
When you hear the gospel proclaimed on Sunday, what is the key unlocking for you personally?

questions.question_text: How is the kingdom of heaven closed and opened by Christian discipline?
questions.answer_text: According to the command of Christ, when those who, under the name of Christians, maintain unchristian doctrine or unchristian conduct, and after repeated brotherly admonition refuse to turn away from their errors and wickedness, are complained of to the Church or to those ordained for that purpose by the Church; and, if they neglect to hear them, are forbidden the use of the Sacraments; whereby they are excluded from the Christian congregation, and by God himself from the kingdom of Christ; and when they promise and show real amendment, they are received again as members of Christ and of his Church.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism describes a process — admonition, escalation, exclusion, restoration. How does seeing it as a process change how you think about church discipline?
The goal is always restoration — 'received again as members.' Does knowing the door is open change how you feel about the discipline?
Let's hold that — discipline is a form of love, not rejection. What would need to change in your church's culture for that to feel true?

questions.question_text: Since we have been delivered from our misery by grace through Christ, without any merit of our own, why must we still do good works?
questions.answer_text: Because Christ, having redeemed us by his blood, also renews us through his Holy Spirit according to his own image, so that with our whole life we may show ourselves thankful to God for his benefits, and he may be praised by us. Furthermore, we ourselves may be assured of our faith by its fruits, and with our godly walk of life we may win our neighbors for Christ.

prompts.prompt_text: Three reasons to do good works: thankfulness, assurance, witness. Which of those three most motivates you, and which feels least real?
The catechism says good works assure us of our faith — not earn it, but confirm it. Have you ever found that to be true?
Let's stay with the catechism's framing — these are works of thankfulness, not obligation. What does it feel like to do something good as a thank-you rather than as a duty?

questions.question_text: Can those who do not turn to God from their thankless, impenitent way of life be saved?
questions.answer_text: Certainly not, for as Holy Scripture says, no unchaste person, no idolater, no adulterer, no thief, no covetous person, no drunkard, no slanderer, no swindler, and so on, shall inherit the kingdom of God.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism uses the word 'thankless' — the issue is not just the sin but the posture toward God beneath it. How does that reframe what repentance requires?
This question seems to reintroduce works into salvation — how does the catechism hold this alongside justification by faith alone?
The list in the answer is convicting — not because we are perfect, but because the pattern of our life reveals our true direction. Where is your life pointed right now?

questions.question_text: How many parts are there to the true repentance or conversion of man?
questions.answer_text: Two: the dying of the old man and the making alive of the new.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism describes repentance as both dying and coming alive — how does the positive half change how you think about what turning from sin means?
Which of the two halves of repentance is more real to you right now — the dying or the being made alive?
Let's stay with the structure — without both halves, what would repentance be missing?

questions.question_text: What is the dying of the old man?
questions.answer_text: To grieve with godly sorrow for our sins and more and more to hate and flee from them.

prompts.prompt_text: Godly sorrow versus worldly sorrow — Paul distinguishes them in 2 Corinthians 7. How do you tell the difference in your own experience?
The catechism says we are to 'hate' our sins — is there a sin you struggle to genuinely hate, and what does that tell you?
Good — let's hear from someone else. What does it feel like to flee from a sin, as opposed to just trying harder not to do it?

questions.question_text: What is the making alive of the new man?
questions.answer_text: A heartfelt joy in God through Christ, and with love and delight to live according to the will of God in all good works.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism says the new life is marked by 'love and delight' in God's will — not reluctant obedience. Where do you feel that delight most, and where does it feel like effort?
If the new life begins with heartfelt joy in God, what gets in the way of that joy for you right now?
Let's hold that. Repentance is not just stopping — it is starting something joyful. How does that reframe what living as a Christian looks like?

questions.question_text: But what are good works?
questions.answer_text: Only those which proceed from true faith, are done according to the law of God, and are done for his glory; and not those based on our own opinion or human tradition.

prompts.prompt_text: Three criteria: from faith, according to God's law, for his glory. How do you evaluate your own actions against those three?
The catechism rules out works 'based on our own opinion' — why is sincerity not enough to make a work good?
Let's stay with the catechism's standard — what work that felt good have you later realized did not meet these criteria?

questions.question_text: What is the law of God?
questions.answer_text: God spoke all these words: I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. You shall have no other gods before me. You shall not make for yourself a carved image... (the Ten Commandments, Exodus 20:1–17 / Deuteronomy 5:6–21)

prompts.prompt_text: The law begins with 'I am the Lord your God who brought you out' — redemption before commandment. How does that preface change how you receive the Ten Commandments?
When you read through the Ten Commandments, which one lands hardest on you right now?
God gives law to his redeemed people — not to earn redemption. What does law as a gift of a gracious God look like compared to law as a demand?

questions.question_text: How are these commandments divided?
questions.answer_text: Into two tables: the first four commandments teach us how we are to relate to God; the last six teach us what we owe our neighbor.

prompts.prompt_text: Love God, love neighbor — the two tables. Which of those two tends to be where you go when life is hard, and which gets neglected?
Jesus said all the law hangs on these two loves. In a typical week, where do you see evidence of both?
Good — let's hear from someone else. If the first table is about our relationship with God, what does failure there do to the second table?

questions.question_text: What does God require in the first commandment?
questions.answer_text: That I, not wanting to endanger my very salvation, avoid and shun all idolatry, sorcery, soothsaying, superstition, prayer to saints or to other creatures. That I rightly know the only true God, trust in him alone, with all humility and patience submit to him, expect all good things only from him, and love, fear, and glorify him with all my heart. In short, that I forsake all creatures rather than do the least thing against his will.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism says to 'expect all good things only from him' — where do you actually expect good things to come from in your daily life?
Idolatry is trusting something else for what only God can give — what functional saviors compete with God in your own heart?
Let's stay with the catechism's summary — forsake all creatures rather than do the least thing against his will. What would it take to live that way?

questions.question_text: What is idolatry?
questions.answer_text: It is to imagine or to have something in which one trusts in place of or alongside of the true God.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism says idolatry can be in the imagination — not just a statue, but a trust in the heart. What does that expand idolatry to include in a modern life?
Paul calls covetousness idolatry. What desire in your life is functioning as a rival to God right now?
Let's land there — idolatry is about trust, not just devotion. What is one practical way you can return trust to God this week?

questions.question_text: What does God require in the second commandment?
questions.answer_text: That we in no way make any image of God, nor worship him in any other way than he has commanded us in his Word.

prompts.prompt_text: God refuses to let us picture him — he prescribes how he is to be worshipped. How do you think about the difference between first and second commandment violations?
Why does God insist that we worship him only as he has commanded, rather than in ways we find meaningful?
Let's stay with the principle — God shapes our worship, not the other way around. What does that say about how we design church services or personal devotion?

questions.question_text: Must images not be made at all?
questions.answer_text: God can and may not be depicted in any way. Creatures may be depicted, but God forbids making images of them in order to worship them or to use them to worship him.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism distinguishes depicting God from depicting creatures — art is not forbidden, but its use in worship is regulated. How does that distinction play out practically in your church?
Some traditions use icons and images devotionally. How do you engage charitably with that practice while holding this catechism answer?
Good — let's hear from someone who finds visual aids helpful in worship. What is the catechism guarding against that might be worth protecting?

questions.question_text: But may not pictures be used in churches in place of books for unlearned people?
questions.answer_text: No, for we should not be wiser than God. He wants his people instructed not by dumb images but by the living preaching of his Word.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism says 'we should not be wiser than God' — he chose words, not images, to reveal himself. What does that say about preaching and Scripture in our age of visual media?
Do you find it easier to connect with God through words, images, music, or silence — and what does the catechism's answer do with that?
Let's land there. The catechism is defending the sufficiency of the Word. How does that confidence shape how much we trust preaching to actually do something?

questions.question_text: What does God require in the third commandment?
questions.answer_text: That we must not blaspheme or misuse the name of God by cursing, perjury, or unnecessary oaths, nor share in such horrible sins by being silent bystanders. In summary, we must not use the holy name of God in any other way than with fear and reverence, so that he may be properly confessed by us, called upon, and praised in all our words and works.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism includes silence — failing to correct blasphemy is itself a violation. How do you navigate that in workplaces or social situations?
Beyond profanity, the catechism is concerned with reverence — what does it look like to use God's name with fear in your ordinary speech?
Let's come back — the commandment is positive as well as negative. What does it look like to use God's name rightly?

questions.question_text: Is the blaspheming of God's name through swearing and cursing such a grievous sin that God is also angry at those who do not prevent and forbid it as much as they can?
questions.answer_text: Undoubtedly, for no sin is greater or provokes God's wrath more than the blaspheming of his name, which is why God commanded that it be punished with death in the Old Testament.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism says there is no sin greater than blaspheming God's name — does that match your moral intuitions, or does it seem overstated?
Why would the severity of a sin be measured by who it is against, not just what is done?
In a culture where God's name is used casually everywhere, how do you cultivate reverence in yourself?

questions.question_text: But may we swear an oath in God's name in a godly manner?
questions.answer_text: Yes, when the government demands it of us, or when necessity requires it, in order thus to maintain and promote fidelity and truth, to the glory of God and to the welfare of our neighbor. Such oath-taking is founded in God's Word and was therefore rightly used by the saints of the Old and New Testaments.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism allows solemn oaths in the name of God — how does that practice reinforce the seriousness of truth-telling in your own life?
When have you made a solemn commitment before God — vows, promises, covenants? What did invoking God's name add to that moment?
Let's stay with what the catechism permits rather than what it forbids — what conditions make an oath godly?

questions.question_text: May we also swear by saints or by any other creatures?
questions.answer_text: No, for a legitimate oath means calling upon God as the only one who knows the heart, and who will punish those who swear falsely, to testify to the truth and to punish me if I swear falsely. Such honor is owed to no creature.

prompts.prompt_text: Oaths invoke God as the witness who sees all and judges — what does that do to the weight of ordinary promises and commitments?
Jesus says 'let your yes be yes' — how does that relate to formal oaths, and what does it say about the standard for everyday speech?
Let's land there — an oath appeals to the God who knows the heart. What would change in how you communicate if you always assumed God was the witness?

questions.question_text: What does God require in the fourth commandment?
questions.answer_text: First, that the ministry of the Gospel and the schools be maintained, and that, especially on the day of rest, I diligently attend the church of God to hear God's Word, to use the sacraments, to call publicly upon God, and to give Christian offerings for the poor. Second, that all the days of my life I rest from my evil works, allow the Lord to work in me through his Spirit, and so begin in this life the eternal Sabbath.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism sees Sunday as a foretaste of the eternal Sabbath — how does that vision change how you approach the Lord's Day?
The catechism says we are to 'allow the Lord to work in us' — not just refrain from work, but actively yield. What does that kind of rest look like for you?
Let's come back to the catechism's two halves — public worship and ongoing daily rest. How do they relate to each other?

questions.question_text: What does God require in the fifth commandment?
questions.answer_text: That I show all honor, love, and faithfulness to my father and mother and to all those in authority over me, submit myself with due obedience to all their good instruction and discipline, and also have patience with their weaknesses and shortcomings, since it is God's will to govern us by their hand.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism extends this commandment beyond parents to all authority — government, church leaders, employers. How do you decide when submission is right and when it has limits?
The catechism includes 'patience with their weaknesses' — authority figures are not perfect. How do you honor someone whose authority you respect but whose character you find difficult?
Good question — the catechism says 'good instruction and discipline.' What happens when the instruction is not good? Let's stay with that limit.

questions.question_text: What does God require in the sixth commandment?
questions.answer_text: That I not revile, hate, insult, or kill my neighbor, neither in thought, nor in word, nor in gesture, much less in deed; whether by myself or through another; but rather lay aside all desire of revenge; and not harm myself nor willfully expose myself to danger. The government also bears the sword to prevent murder.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism includes thought and word alongside deed — murder begins in the heart. Where does that locate the battle for you?
