The catechism also includes self-harm and reckless self-endangerment — how does caring for your own life fit into loving your neighbor?
Let's stay with 'laying aside all desire of revenge' — what does that require from you practically when someone has wronged you?

questions.question_text: But this commandment seems to speak only of killing?
questions.answer_text: In forbidding murder, God teaches us that he hates the root of murder: envy, hatred, anger, desire of revenge; and he regards all these as murder.

prompts.prompt_text: John says whoever hates his brother is a murderer — that is a serious claim. How does hearing that change how you think about anger?
God hates the root, not just the fruit — why does the internal matter as much as the external action to him?
Is there an envy or anger you are carrying right now that the catechism would say God regards as seriously as you regard murder?

questions.question_text: Is it enough, then, that we do not kill our neighbor in any such way?
questions.answer_text: No, for when God condemns envy, hatred, and anger, he commands us to love our neighbor as ourselves, to show patience, peace, gentleness, mercy, and all kindness toward him, and to prevent his harm as much as we can; also to do good even to our enemies.

prompts.prompt_text: Not harming is not enough — we must do good even to enemies. Who in your life is hardest to do good toward right now?
The catechism lists patience, peace, gentleness, mercy, and kindness — which of those is hardest for you to show consistently?
Let's hold that list. Patience, peace, gentleness, mercy, kindness. Which one is a discipline for you this week?

questions.question_text: What does the seventh commandment teach us?
questions.answer_text: That all unchastity is condemned by God and that therefore we must thoroughly detest it and live chastely and modestly, whether in holy marriage or in the single life.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism applies chastity to both married and single life — how is faithfulness in marriage and faithfulness in singleness related?
The catechism says to 'thoroughly detest' sexual sin — not just avoid it. How does that level of active rejection differ from passive resistance?
Let's stay with the catechism's positive vision — what does chaste and modest living look like in practice in today's culture?

questions.question_text: Does God forbid only adultery and such gross sins in this commandment?
questions.answer_text: Since both our body and soul are temples of the Holy Spirit, he commands us to keep both pure and holy. God therefore forbids all unchaste actions, gestures, words, thoughts, desires, and whatever may attract a man to such things.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism includes words, gestures, and things that attract — the commandment reaches into media, entertainment, and imagination. How do you apply that practically?
The catechism grounds sexual ethics in the body being a temple of the Spirit — how does that theological grounding change the motivation for purity?
Good — let's hear from someone who finds this area of the law either more demanding or more freeing than they expected.

questions.question_text: What does God forbid in the eighth commandment?
questions.answer_text: God forbids not only those thefts and robberies which civil authorities punish, but he regards as theft also all wicked tricks and devices by which we aim at appropriating to ourselves our neighbor's goods, whether by force or under color of right, such as dishonest weights and measures, unjust prices, deceptive merchandise or money, usury, or by any other means forbidden by God; as also all covetousness and abuse and waste of his gifts.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism includes 'unjust prices' and 'deceptive merchandise' as forms of theft — how does that apply to modern business practices you encounter?
The catechism adds 'waste of his gifts' — misusing what God gave you counts as stealing from him. How does that change how you think about your resources?
Let's stay with the catechism's breadth — this commandment covers legal and illegal forms of taking. What legal practices might still violate it?

questions.question_text: But what does God require of you in this commandment?
questions.answer_text: That I further the profit of my neighbor wherever I can and may; that I deal with him as I would like him to deal with me; and that I work faithfully so that I may be able to give to those in need.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism's positive command is to further your neighbor's profit — not just protect his property, but actively help him flourish. How does that shape your work?
We work faithfully 'so that we may give to those in need' — giving is the goal of working, not just personal security. How does that reframe your relationship to money?
Let's land there — what is one neighbor whose profit you could actively further this week?

questions.question_text: What is required in the ninth commandment?
questions.answer_text: That I bear false witness against no one, twist no one's words, be no backbiter or slanderer, join in condemning no one unheard or rashly; but that on pain of God's fierce wrath I avoid all lying and deceit as the very works of the devil; and that in judicial and all other matters I love, speak, and stand for the truth; and that I confess and make known, as best I can, the honor and good character of my neighbor.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism includes 'joining in condemning no one unheard' — how often do social media and group conversations violate that principle?
The catechism calls us to 'make known the honor and good character of our neighbor' — when did you last actively speak well of someone who needed defending?
Let's come back — the catechism links lying to the devil. What is it about falsehood that is so fundamentally anti-God?

questions.question_text: What does the tenth commandment require of us?
questions.answer_text: That not even the least inclination or thought against any of God's commandments shall ever arise in our hearts, but that with our whole heart we shall continually hate all sin and take delight in all righteousness.

prompts.prompt_text: The tenth commandment reaches into desire — not just action or word but inclination. What does it do to your self-understanding to know that God's law goes that deep?
Paul says he would not have known covetousness was sin without this commandment. What does the law reveal in you that you might prefer not to see?
Let's stay with 'delight in all righteousness' — the catechism is describing a heart transformation, not just rule-keeping. What would need to change in you for that to be true?

questions.question_text: But can those who are converted to God keep these commandments perfectly?
questions.answer_text: No, for even the holiest men, while in this life, have only a small beginning of this obedience; yet so that with a sincere resolution they begin to live, not only according to some, but all the commandments of God.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism says even the holiest have only 'a small beginning' — how does that honest assessment change what you expect from yourself and from other Christians?
A sincere resolve to keep all the commandments is what the catechism looks for — not perfection, but direction. Where is your life pointed?
Let's hear from someone else — does 'small beginning' feel discouraging or freeing to you?

questions.question_text: Why then does God have the Ten Commandments preached so strictly, since no one can keep them in this life?
questions.answer_text: First, that all our life long we may become more and more aware of our sinful nature, and so become more eager to seek the forgiveness of sins and righteousness in Christ. Second, that we constantly endeavor and pray to God for the grace of the Holy Spirit, so that more and more we may be renewed in the image of God, until after this life we attain the goal of full perfection.

prompts.prompt_text: The law's purpose is to make us more eager for Christ and more dependent on the Spirit — how is that a different posture toward law than trying harder?
Has studying the Ten Commandments over these weeks made you more aware of sin, more eager for forgiveness, or more dependent on grace?
Let's land there — the law is preached strictly so we run to Christ, not away from him. How does that reframe what it feels like to hear a convicting sermon?

questions.question_text: Why is prayer necessary for Christians?
questions.answer_text: Because prayer is the main part of the thankfulness which God requires of us; and also because God will give his grace and Holy Spirit only to those who with sincere longing continually ask him for these gifts and thank him for them.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism says prayer is the main expression of thankfulness — how does that reframe prayer from request-making to something else?
The catechism says God gives the Spirit to those who 'continually ask' — what does that imply about the relationship between your prayer life and your experience of the Spirit?
Let's come back — if prayer is primarily thankfulness, what happens to how you pray when life is painful?

questions.question_text: What belongs to a prayer which is pleasing to God and which he will hear?
questions.answer_text: First, that we from the heart call upon the one true God only, who has revealed himself in his Word, for all that he has commanded us to pray. Second, that we thoroughly know our need and misery, so that we may humble ourselves before God's majesty. Third, that we be firmly assured that he, notwithstanding that we are unworthy of it, will, for the sake of Christ our Lord, certainly hear our prayer, as he has promised us in his Word.

prompts.prompt_text: Three conditions: right address, genuine need, confident assurance. Which of those three most shapes your actual prayers, and which do you neglect?
The catechism says to 'thoroughly know our need and misery' — how honest are you in prayer about how desperate you actually are?
The catechism grounds assurance in Christ, not in our worthiness — when prayer feels hollow, what does this answer say to lean on?

questions.question_text: What did God command us to pray for?
questions.answer_text: All the things we need for body and soul, which Christ our Lord has comprised in the prayer which he himself has taught us.

prompts.prompt_text: God commands us to ask for what we need for both body and soul — how well does your prayer life cover both?
Jesus gave us a prayer to pray — why is it significant that the form of our prayer was given to us rather than invented by us?
Good — let's hear from someone who finds the Lord's Prayer either very alive or quite routine in their practice.

questions.question_text: What is this prayer?
questions.answer_text: Our Father who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name, thy kingdom come, thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven. Give us this day our daily bread, and forgive us our debts as we forgive our debtors, and do not lead us into temptation, but deliver us from evil. For thine is the kingdom and the power and the glory forever. Amen.

prompts.prompt_text: Read the Lord's Prayer together slowly, then ask: which petition most pressed on you today and why?
The prayer begins with 'our' — not my. What does the communal opening do to how you pray even when alone?
Let's keep this prayer with us through the next several Lord's Days as we unpack each petition.

questions.question_text: Why has Christ commanded us to address God as Our Father?
questions.answer_text: That at the very beginning of our prayer he might awaken in us the childlike reverence and trust toward God which should be basic to our prayer — namely, that God has become our Father through Christ and will much less deny us what we ask of him in faith than our fathers would refuse us earthly things.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism says 'Our Father' is meant to awaken trust at the very start of prayer — how does the name you use for God shape what you expect from him?
For some people, the word 'Father' is complicated by earthly experience — how do you navigate that, and what does the catechism say God is like as a Father?
Let's stay with the catechism's claim — God is more willing to give than earthly fathers. What does that level of generosity invite you to ask for?

questions.question_text: Why is there added: who art in heaven?
questions.answer_text: That we might have no earthly conception of the heavenly majesty of God, and from his almighty power expect everything needed for body and soul.

prompts.prompt_text: Father and heavenly — intimate and transcendent at once. Which of those two tends to dominate your picture of God, and what gets lost when you overemphasize one?
The catechism says we should expect 'everything needed for body and soul' from his almighty power — what need feels too big or too small to bring to a God like this?
Good — let's hear from someone else. What does 'in heaven' do to your experience of prayer right now?

questions.question_text: What is the first petition?
questions.answer_text: Hallowed be thy name. That is: Grant us first of all that we may rightly know thee, and sanctify, glorify, and praise thee in all thy works, in which thy power, goodness, justice, mercy, and truth shine forth; and further, that we may so order our whole life — our thoughts, words, and deeds — that thy name may never be blasphemed but may be honored and praised on our account.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism says we pray for God's name to be hallowed through our lives — this petition is about our witness as much as about God. How does that land?
We ask to 'rightly know' God first — knowledge before praise. Is there something about God you want to know better before you can praise him well?
Let's stay with the catechism's expansion — this is a petition for our whole life to display God's glory. What would it take for your week to honor his name?

questions.question_text: What is the second petition?
questions.answer_text: Thy kingdom come. That is: Rule us so by thy Word and Spirit that we may submit ourselves more and more to thee; preserve and increase thy Church; destroy the works of the devil and all violence that exalts itself against thee; and do away with all wicked counsel that is taken against thy holy Word, until the fullness of thy kingdom comes in which thou wilt be all in all.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism says the kingdom comes as we submit to God's Word and Spirit — it starts in us before it transforms the world. Where is that submission most needed in your life right now?
This petition asks God to destroy the works of the devil — have you ever prayed that specifically about something in your own life or community?
The catechism ends this petition with 'all in all' — when everything is finally subjected to God. What gives you hope that his kingdom is actually advancing right now?

questions.question_text: What is the third petition?
questions.answer_text: Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven. That is: Grant that we and all men may renounce our own will and obey thy will, which alone is good, without murmuring; so that each may perform the duties of his office and calling as willingly and faithfully as the angels in heaven.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism says angels obey without murmuring — that is the standard for our obedience. What would it take for you to obey your calling as willingly as that?
We renounce our own will — is there a place in your life right now where your will and God's will are in conflict?
Let's stay with the catechism's vision — not reluctant compliance but willing faithfulness in our particular calling. What is your calling, and how well are you fulfilling it?

questions.question_text: What is the fourth petition?
questions.answer_text: Give us this day our daily bread. That is: Be pleased to provide us with all things necessary for the body, so that we may thereby acknowledge that thou art the only fountain of all good, and that without thy blessing neither our care and labor, nor thy gifts, can profit us; and therefore that we may withdraw our trust from all creatures and place it only in thee.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism says even our labor cannot profit us without God's blessing — how does that shape how you think about work, income, and security?
Where do you actually place your trust for daily provision — in your job, savings, or somewhere else? What would it look like to move that trust to God?
Let's hear from someone who has experienced the fragility of material security. What did that do to your praying?

questions.question_text: What is the fifth petition?
questions.answer_text: Forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors. That is: Be pleased, for the sake of Christ's blood, not to impute to us, miserable sinners, our transgressions nor the evil which still clings to us; as we also find this evidence of thy grace in us, that it is our firm resolve to forgive our neighbor.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism ties our forgiveness to our forgiving — not as earning, but as evidence of grace received. How does the link between the two affect how you pray this petition?
The catechism says the evil 'still clings to us' — not just past sins but present struggle. How does confessing that ongoing reality change your posture before God?
Let's stay with the uncomfortable question — is there anyone you have not forgiven, and can you honestly pray this petition right now?

questions.question_text: What is the sixth petition?
questions.answer_text: And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil. That is: Since we are so weak in ourselves that we cannot stand for one moment, and since our sworn enemies — the devil, the world, and our own flesh — assail us without ceasing, be pleased to preserve and strengthen us by the power of thy Holy Spirit, so that we may not go down to defeat in this spiritual warfare, but may constantly and strenuously resist our foes, until we finally obtain the complete victory.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism says we cannot stand for one moment on our own — how honest is that assessment of yourself, and what does it do to how you face temptation?
Three enemies: the devil, the world, and our own flesh. Which of those three is bearing down on you most right now?
The catechism promises 'complete victory' at the end — how does that destination change how you fight the battle today?

questions.question_text: How do you close this prayer?
questions.answer_text: For thine is the kingdom and the power and the glory forever. That is: All this we pray of thee, because thou, as our all-powerful King, art both willing and able to give us all good things; and because thy holy name, and not we ourselves, should be praised forever.

prompts.prompt_text: The doxology grounds confidence: he is willing and able. Which of those two do you find harder to believe about God — his willingness or his ability?
The catechism says his name, not ours, should be praised — prayer ends with doxology, not with us. Why does that matter for how we feel when prayers seem unanswered?
Good — let's hear from someone else. What does it do to your praying to end with praise rather than with your requests?

questions.question_text: What does the word Amen mean?
questions.answer_text: Amen means: So shall it truly be. For my prayer is much more certainly heard of God than I am persuaded in my heart that I desire these things of him.

prompts.prompt_text: The catechism says God hears your prayer more certainly than you feel your own desire — how does that reverse the usual logic of confidence in prayer?
Amen is an act of trust, not a feeling — you say 'so shall it truly be' even when you are not sure. Has there been a prayer where you said Amen without conviction, and what happened?
Let's end here — the catechism ends with certainty, not with our feelings. After 52 Lord's Days, what is the one truth you most want to carry forward?
